master.title: Daily headlines from Japan
master.content:
Japan, US, South Korea agree to step up security cooperation

The foreign ministers of Japan, the US and South Korea met in Hawaii on Saturday and issued a joint statement condemning the recent series of missile launches by North Korea and pledging to strengthen their trilateral security cooperation to enhance deterrence. It was the first time in three years that the three countries issued a joint paper after a foreign ministers' meeting. FM Yoshimasa Hayashi, US Secretary of State Antony Blinken and South Korean FM Chung Eui-yong also indirectly warned China against exerting military pressure on Taiwan. The ministers also discussed the Ukraine crisis. (Asahi, Mainichi, Tokyo Shimbun, Nikkei)

G7 vows collective economic sanctions if Russian aggression escalates

The G7 finance ministers issued a joint statement Monday stating their readiness to impose economic sanctions against Russia if the country invades Ukraine. It was the first time the finance ministers referred to the possibility of sanctions since tensions began to mount. (Mainichi, Nikkei)

Government to drop some penalties in planned economic security legislation

In response to concerns expressed by the business community and junior coalition partner Komeito, the government is looking to drop part of the penalties it had planned to include in new economic security legislation to be submitted to the current session of the Diet, media reported. According to the report, one penalty that will be dropped is the idea of a fine of up to 300,000 JPY (2,273 EUR) for noncompliance by importers or sellers of key materials such as chips with government minister demands to see relevant documents or reports. Businesses have in recent weeks said they are worried that the legislation would be too strict and stifle business activity. (Asahi)

Justice Ministry panel urges changes to 19th century paternity rules

An advisory panel to the Justice Ministry submitted to the minister on Monday its recommendations for revisions to the Civil Code that include a call for ending the rule dating back to 1898 that presumes a baby born within 300 days of its mother's divorce is the child of her previous husband. The panel proposed an addendum so that if the mother has remarried by the time of the birth, her new husband would be the father. While the concept is widely viewed as something from a bygone era, similar efforts some 15 years ago were blocked by conservatives, who argued that it would encourage extramarital affairs. Some women, who did not want their ex-husband to be the legal father, have opted not to register the births, leaving the children with no family record or nationality. Another key point in Monday's proposals was that pregnant women need not wait 100 days after getting divorced before remarrying. (Asahi, Sankei)

Russian skater can continue competing in Beijing Games despite doping allegations

All major national dailies reported on their front pages that Russian teenage figure skater Kamila Valieva has been cleared to compete in today's women's single skating competition at the Beijing Olympics. Japanese media have closely followed developments in the saga, given keen public interest in the sport. Japan won a bronze medal in the team skate competition last week, while Russia, with Valieva, won gold. On Monday, the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) ruled that Valieva can compete for the remainder of this year's Games, despite testing positive for a prohibited substance before the Olympics. (Asahi, Yomiuri, Mainichi, Sankei)

Europe a late arrival in wooing TMSC (Nikkei, 880 words w/photo and table)

Prepared based on the vernacular press by Mari Koseki, Chief Press Officer, Political, Press and Information Section, EU Delegation to Japan
